newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian protest leader takes reins of reform.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian protest leader takes reins of reform.

text.p: Ivan Kostov, nominated as Bulgarian prime minister on Thursday, led his fractious reformist coalition to election victory but now faces the challenge of reviving the economy and improving his compatriots' lives.
"We must lead Bulgaria out of the catastrophe. We must. And we will do it," Kostov told supporters in an incantation repeated throughout the election campaign.
For 30 days in January and February, Kostov ignored bouts of flu and freezing temperatures to address rallies and lead marches which finally toppled the Socialist government.
He galvanised 15 parties into the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) coalition which won 52 percent of the vote in Saturday's election.
"The future Bulgarian cabinet will rely on the reformist majority in society which is expected to support its reforms and to save Bulgaria," Kostov told reporters on Thursday.

A vegetarian who likes to jog, he is now in charge of an ambitious reform package sealed between the International Monetary Fund and the interim cabinet, which aims to propel the debt-ridden nation out of crisis.
"He's easy to work with as long as you know he's in charge. He has a sense of humour, is polite with friends but he can be distant and cold with people he doesn't like," said one Kostov associate.
Colleagues say the 47-year-old prime minister has a stong ego, but he will need all his self-confidence for the difficult task ahead.
Seven years after the fall of communism, Bulgaria still talks of market reforms in the future tense.
Kostov has said that one of his priorities is curbing organised crime, hoping to counter opponents' allegations that the UDF has accepted funds and advice from shady businesses.

Restoring confidence in the financial system and advancing Bulgaria's case for membership of the European Union and NATO are also high on the agenda, though the latter risks upsetting Russia, with which Bulgaria still has close economic ties.
Kostov has a tough act to follow in interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski, Sofia's popular UDF mayor, who has led a succesful caretaker cabinet since the Socialists stepped down in February.
Kostov was born in Sofia on December 23, 1949. He has two daughters and is married to Elena Grigorova.
An associate professor of economics, he has served twice as finance minister since the fall of one-party communist rule in 1989 -- once in a 1990 caretaker government and then in 1991.
Some of the measures which a Kostov government would have to take would test the patience of the crowds which have cheered him so far.

A plan for a currency board, a fixed exchange rate mechanism to stop the fall of the lev and curb inflation, would put a stop to irresponsible printing of money but could force deep jobs cuts and curb government spending on social benefits.
